name: Rasagiline
originator: Technion – Israel Institute of Technology (Moussa Youdim, John Finberg) and Teva Pharmaceutical Industries

discovery.by: Moussa Youdim and John Finberg, Technion, with Teva
discovery.note: Developed as a propargylamine MAO-B inhibitor that, unlike selegiline, is not metabolised to amphetamines.

tagline: Once-daily MAO-B inhibitor for Parkinson's disease, developed in Israel
summary: Rasagiline is a second-generation irreversible MAO-B inhibitor used once daily as monotherapy in early Parkinson's disease or as an adjunct to levodopa. It was developed at the Technion with Teva and is now generic.
mechanism: Rasagiline binds covalently to the flavin cofactor of MAO-B, irreversibly blocking the oxidative deamination of dopamine in the striatum and so increasing synaptic dopamine.

Its main metabolite, 1(R)-aminoindan, is not an amphetamine, avoiding the amphetamine-like metabolites of selegiline. Laboratory studies suggested neuroprotective properties, but disease modification has not been proven in humans.
uses: Parkinson's disease (monotherapy and adjunct to levodopa)

history.title: US approval
history.detail: The FDA approves Azilect for Parkinson's disease.

history.title: ADAGIO
history.detail: A delayed-start trial (Olanow et al., NEJM) gives ambiguous results: 1 mg met criteria for possible disease modification, 2 mg did not.

history.title: FDA declines disease-modifying claim
history.detail: An FDA advisory committee votes against a label claim of slowing Parkinson's disease progression.

history.title: Generics
history.detail: Generic rasagiline becomes available in the US.

pk.half_life: about 0.6–2 hours; enzyme inhibition lasts much longer

serious: Serotonin syndrome with serotonergic drugs or pethidine

facts: Rasagiline is the R-enantiomer of N-propargyl-1-aminoindan; the S-enantiomer is far less potent at MAO-B.
